title: Guild-Issued Credentials That Beat Free Badges
one_liner: Turn illustrator, photographer, translator and indie-label associations into verifiers that issue portable 'real working creator' credentials.
customer: Trade associations, unions and guilds with 1,000-50,000 members who need visible AI-era member value. Second-side buyers are contests, publishers, agencies and brands that want to check a creator quickly.
problem: Insiders assume a universal proof-of-personhood is needed, like World's iris scans or platform badges. But Spotify says over 99% of artists listeners search for are already verified, so a free badge says nothing about who is a working professional. The brief flags that a paid credential must beat the free native one, and it cannot do so on 'is human' alone.
solution: A white-label service where the guild verifies members using its own dues records and portfolio review, and we issue portable credentials. These are W3C verifiable credentials, Bluesky trusted-verifier labels, a signed .well-known file for members' websites and an embeddable badge. A lookup API lets buyers and contest platforms verify membership and standing. Guilds also get a public directory.
why_now: Org-issued verification became a working pattern on Bluesky in 2025, and TikTok joining C2PA in Jul 2026 shows provenance moving to the mainstream. Guild members are demanding concrete AI-era protection, and platform badges are free and universal, so they cannot signal professional standing.
revenue_model: Association license of $5-25k/year, $1-3 per member per year for issuance, and lookup fees for enterprise buyers such as contests and agencies.
non_obvious_insight: The value of verification comes from the stakes and scarcity of the issuer, not from cryptography. Guilds already own the membership record and the trust, and a platform that gives everyone a badge cannot compete with that.
first_30_days: Pitch 20 mid-size associations with a one-page offer: a 3-week pilot of 100 verified members on Bluesky and their own websites. Charge a $2-5k pilot fee, and aim to have one association make it a renewal benefit.

title: Bank-Accepted $1,500 Diligence for Main Street Deals
angle: Pairing 1: SMB back office/compliance/marketing/succession x Trust & verification markets (succession x audits)
one_liner: A fixed-price, CPA-signed mini quality-of-earnings pack that brokers attach to sub-$1M business listings so SBA lenders and first-time buyers can close deals that currently die at diligence.
customer: Business brokers listing $150K-$1M cash-flow businesses (pay about $995 per listing to pre-certify), first-time individual buyers (pay $1,500 at letter of intent), and community-bank SBA lenders who accept the format.
problem: Boomer-owned Main Street businesses (HVAC, laundromats, landscaping, small clinics) sell on seller-supplied P&Ls and add-backs because a real quality-of-earnings review costs roughly $15K-50K (prior knowledge), which is more than many deals can bear. Search-fund capital targets $5-50M companies, so no formal capital or diligence product exists below $1M (brief inference). Deals die late or close on bad numbers.
solution: A five-day standardized pack. AI ties out bank feeds, POS data and sales-tax filings to IRS tax transcripts (hard to forge), samples add-backs, checks customer and revenue concentration, runs a reviews-and-traffic authenticity check (bought reviews and followers inflate perceived brand value), scans liens, licenses and litigation, and produces an owner-dependence score. A partner CPA reviews and signs. The signed pack attaches to the listing and is reusable across buyers.
why_now: SBA loosened acquisition financing on 2026-07-04 (7(a) and 504 loans can be combined for up to $10M of SBA-backed financing). AI-forged P&Ls and bank-statement PDFs are now trivial to produce (prior knowledge), so lenders and buyers need evidence that survives forgery. CPA supply is flat at about 678K, so cheap AI tie-out plus a reviewing CPA is the only way to serve small deals. Bench's Dec 2024 collapse showed sellers' books can be trapped inside a vendor.
revenue_model: $1,500 buyer-paid report or $995 broker pre-certification per listing, plus a $250 lender-portal fee. Roughly 3 CPA hours per pack plus software gives about 65% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: The deal-killer is not the price of diligence, it is that diligence gets redone for every buyer. Certifying the listing once turns a per-buyer cost into a per-listing asset that brokers will pay for because it buys deal certainty. Tax transcripts plus bank feeds are also the only evidence AI cannot cheaply fake.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 freelance ex-QoE CPAs and ask 5 regional business brokers for active listings. Run 10 free packs in exchange for case studies and lender feedback, then charge $995 per listing. Walk the format past 2 SBA Preferred Lenders at community banks so 'lender-accepted' is true by month 3.

title: Half-Plate Menus for GLP-1 Diners
one_liner: A menu-engineering and POS program that turns GLP-1 diners into incremental visits through protein-first half portions.
customer: Multi-unit casual-dining and fast-casual operators with 20-300 locations.
problem: GLP-1 households cut restaurant spend about 8%, yet 48% of users say they would dine out more if smaller portions were offered.
solution: Design a 'Half-Plate' section (65-70% of full price, protein-forward, fiber-tuned), integrate it in the POS, and measure incremental visits and margin per cover.
why_now: About 12% of Americans use a GLP-1 and the oral Wegovy pill launched in January 2026 at $149-299/month, so the segment is now big enough for a dedicated menu line.
revenue_model: Per-location monthly fee plus a performance share of measured incremental visits.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume smaller portions cannibalize revenue, but restaurant labor and rent are per-cover costs. A visit at 70% of the check with lower food cost beats losing the visit at 100%.
first_30_days: Sign two regional chains for a 10-store test of a Half-Plate section and set up a simple visit-frequency and basket dashboard from POS exports.

title: Flat-Fee Authenticity Reports for Family-Law Attorneys
one_liner: 48-hour, court-ready analyses of disputed audio, video and screenshots at $400-900, instead of $10K expert engagements.
customer: Solo and small-firm family-law, employment and landlord-tenant attorneys, HR investigators, school districts, and small police departments.
problem: Fake voicemails, cloned-voice threats and doctored screenshots now appear as evidence in custody and workplace disputes, and real evidence gets dismissed as fake. Forensic experts cost $5-15K and take weeks, which prices out most cases. Evidence-rule committees are debating standards for machine-generated evidence.
solution: Upload a file for automated provenance checks (metadata, re-encoding traces, C2PA), multi-detector analysis, voice consistency against known samples, and platform-screenshot forensics. A human examiner reviews and signs, and the output is a plain-language report, declaration template, methodology and error-rate disclosure.
why_now: Voice cloning takes 3 seconds of audio, which floods lower-stakes disputes with synthetic-evidence claims. Courts are asking who verified the evidence, and no one serves the long tail of small cases.
revenue_model: $400-900 per report, $299 per month for firms including 3 reports, and expert-testimony upsells at about $3K.
non_obvious_insight: The market is not detection accuracy but the cost of access to a credentialed examiner. Demand is two-sided: people accused of faking real evidence also need authenticity certificates. The human sign-off is the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 contract forensic examiners. Build the intake page and report template. Run bar-association webinars and get 10 family-law firms to buy 3 pilot reports each.

title: W-2 Employer-of-Record for AI-Training Experts
one_liner: A task-metered payroll, benefits and contract layer that lets data vendors and labs engage expert contractors as short-term employees without the misclassification and breach exposure of 1099 mass onboarding.
customer: Second-tier human-data vendors (challengers to the Mercor-scale players) and enterprise AI teams running expert-evaluation programs pay an 8-12% margin over payroll.
problem: A class action alleges Surge AI misclassified annotators, Mercor's reported breach exposed about 40k contractors' voice samples, and contractors report declining pay and stress. Enterprise buyers in banking and healthcare won't sign vendors lacking employment and security controls. Standard EOR services can't handle 2-40 hour micro-engagements.
solution: Instant W-2 onboarding across 50 states, with per-task hourly pay, automatic state paid-sick-leave accrual, workers' comp and unemployment tax handled. A data-security wrapper (SSO, ephemeral biometric handling) and portable pay stubs for the worker's income verification round it out.
why_now: Misclassification suits and breach fallout landed in 2025-26, enterprises are now buying expert data and demanding compliance, and a multi-million expert contractor pool has appeared with unprecedented scale.
revenue_model: 8-12% of payroll plus a per-worker admin fee.
non_obvious_insight: Leading marketplaces prefer contractor status because they keep 30-40%, but enterprise and regulated buyers can't absorb the liability. Being the plumbing for challengers, not another marketplace, gives them the enterprise wedge against incumbents.
first_30_days: White-label an existing PEO or EOR to avoid licensing. Sign two small vendors (legal, medical or finance data) for a pilot cohort of 50 W-2 experts. Publish a misclassification-risk checklist to generate inbound.

title: Evacuation Lift Registry Ending Double-Booked Buses
one_liner: A neutral county-level registry that guarantees each ambulance, wheelchair van and bus seat is promised to only one nursing home per storm, paid for by facilities and by carriers who finally get standby retainers.
customer: Paying: multi-site nursing home and assisted-living operators (SaaS per facility) and ambulance/NEMT/charter-bus operators (platform fee on standby retainers). Sponsoring: county emergency managers and healthcare coalitions using preparedness grants.
problem: The CMS emergency preparedness rule makes every facility hold transportation agreements, but no one checks whether the same 40 wheelchair vans and ambulances are 'contracted' by 300 facilities. GAO and post-Katrina research found carriers holding contracts with many facilities in one community, which works for a single-building evacuation and collapses when a whole county goes at once. Facilities learn at H-48 that their contract is one of a dozen identical promises. Carriers do not honor a promise they were never paid to hold.
solution: Borrow the military's lift-allocation discipline, where an asset can appear on the movement plan only once. Facilities reserve capacity by resident mix (ambulatory, wheelchair, stretcher, oxygen or vent-dependent), not by 'beds'. The registry totals promised demand against real vehicle capacity by county and flags oversubscription weeks before the season, then matches the gap to out-of-region carriers on paid standby. At activation it issues a departure-window movement table so convoys do not collide, plus manifest and accountability packets for each facility. Before activation it stores only aggregate counts by acuity, not PHI, which keeps HIPAA scope small.
why_now: The President's FEMA Review Council final report (May 7, 2026) recommends disaster response be 'locally executed, state managed, federally supported'. Counties and healthcare coalitions are inheriting logistics they never staffed, with less federal backfill. It is peak hurricane season, and post-acute care closures and consolidation are concentrating residents into fewer, larger buildings.
revenue_model: $150-400 per facility per month. Carriers pay 8-12% on standby retainers the platform brokers, which they never received before. Optional county or coalition license of $25-100k a year, funded by ASPR HPP or EMPG grants. Later, add-ons for dialysis centers, group homes and inpatient rehab.
non_obvious_insight: Vehicles are not the shortage. Unique promises are. Every evacuation failure post-mortem says 'not enough buses', but the fleet often exists and is simply committed many times over. Military movement planners never let one lift asset appear twice on a time-phased deployment plan, while civilian planners have nobody whose job is to check. Loading time is also the hidden constraint: a stretcher resident takes about 20 minutes to load, so acuity mix, not headcount, determines how many vehicles you need.
first_30_days: Pick one storm-prone county cluster (Tampa Bay, coastal Carolinas or Louisiana parishes). Ask 10 facilities to share their transport MOUs, which they must keep on file for CMS surveys anyway. Build the overlap heat map by hand in a spreadsheet, for example 'nine of your ten facilities are promised the same carrier'. Take it to the county emergency manager and the healthcare coalition coordinator. Convert 3-5 facilities to a paid pilot at about $200 a month and sign 2 carriers to retainer contracts. Build the product as Airtable plus a simple web form before writing real software.

title: File-Cabinet-to-Pipeline Digitization Crew
one_liner: A mobile scan-and-extract crew that turns a newly acquired trades company's filing cabinets and paper job files into a clean customer and equipment-age database plus a ready-to-run replacement and membership campaign.
customer: Acquirers of legacy HVAC, plumbing, roofing, pest, electrical and garage-door companies (search funders, holdcos, PE add-on platforms). The buyer pays a fixed fee plus a share of revenue from jobs sold off the output. Brokers are a secondary channel, using it as sell-side data-room prep.
problem: Acquired trades firms often run on paper, desk phones and old PCs, so the owner cannot see permit errors, warranty problems or job margins. Any AI, field-service software or roll-up integration needs structured data first. Meanwhile decades of installs sit in file drawers as an unused equipment-age database.
solution: A two-person crew with document scanners and phone capture spends 5-10 days on site. Vision-model extraction pulls customer, address, equipment make/model/serial, install date, service history, warranty status and membership status. Output is import-ready for ServiceTitan, Jobber, Housecall Pro and QuickBooks, plus an 'asset-age' list: homes with systems older than a set threshold, expiring warranties, lapsed maintenance customers and contract renewals. It includes a letter/SMS campaign and prepaid-membership offer templates, with job tagging so results are measured.
why_now: Handwriting and form extraction from photos became accurate and cheap in 2025-2026. Bain's 2026 GP outlook says 39% of GPs expect no material financial impact from AI on portfolio companies this year, and Bain's midyear report says leaders redesign workflows rather than layering tools on top. Both point to data readiness as the gap. First-time buyers of small trades firms are more numerous than ever, and each faces the same digitization backlog.
revenue_model: $8-15K fixed fee per business, plus 8-10% of first-year revenue from jobs tagged to campaigns generated from the output. Sell-side version for brokers: $3-5K data-room prep before listing.
non_obvious_insight: What looks like clutter is a proprietary, geocoded equipment-age database of thousands of households, the highest-intent lead list in the trades, and the buyer paid for it in the purchase price without knowing. Rob Brooks found '30,000 customer records' in filing cabinets, 13-year-old computers and desk phones, could not see permit or warranty problems until he digitized, and reached $1.3M EBITDA from $340K SDE in 14 months with about 800 customers prepaying three years of membership (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/rob-brooks-gary-air). Winsor Fireform's buyers spent seven months digitizing roughly 90% paper records (https://acquiringminds.co/articles/andrew-sova-alex-clark-winsor-fireform-novo-foundry). Tew & Taylor ran on Excel and mailed checks, creating a large receivables backlog (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). Bain's GP outlook notes 39% of GPs see no material AI impact on portfolios in 2026 (https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equitys-reality-check-gp-outlook-2026/). Every buyer solved digitization ad hoc, and none treated the archive as revenue.
first_30_days: Pick HVAC in one metro. Find 3 recent small-business buyers through ETA communities and brokers, and offer one a near-cost pilot. Scan and extract 2,000 records in 3 days, mail letters or SMS to the oldest-equipment homes, and count booked calls per 500 contacts. Publish the result as a case study, then price the service at $8-15K plus revenue share. Meanwhile approach 5 HVAC business brokers with the sell-side data-room version.

title: Cloud Machine Shop for High-School Shop Class
one_liner: Students design parts, watch real CNC machines cut them live at a partner job shop, and receive the parts by mail, so any school gets a hands-on manufacturing lab without machines or instructors.
customer: High-school and community-college CTE and robotics programs (per-project fees, often funded by CTE grants); job shops sponsor for recruiting.
problem: Manufacturing has openings, but CNC labs cost $100k+ and need instructors who are scarce, so rural and small schools cannot offer them. AI can now generate designs but students never touch real machining. Hands-on work is also the AI-resilient part of learning.
solution: A web portal: design in browser CAD with AI assist, automatic manufacturability checks and CAM by the partner shop, a scheduled live-stream slot where the machine cuts the student's part with a shop mentor narrating, then shipment. Curriculum aligns to entry-level machining credential levels and gives teachers a dashboard.
why_now: Text-to-CAD and instant-quote manufacturing platforms are good enough in 2026, streaming is trivial, and job shops have idle off-peak capacity and hiring pain. School AI pauses and screen fatigue make hands-on offerings attractive.
revenue_model: $25-60 per student project, $3-6k per classroom per year, plus recruiting sponsorship from job shops and manufacturer associations.
non_obvious_insight: Equipment and instructors are the constraint, not student interest. Machines already run from files, so the lab can be teleported, and idle night-shift capacity is a free asset that the shop's hiring pain will pay to use.
first_30_days: Partner with one local job shop with a couple of machines available off-peak. Recruit 5 CTE or robotics teachers. Run a 3-week design-and-cut unit at $30 per student and measure engagement. Map the unit to a machining credential standard.

title: Battery-Buffered Induction Kitchens for LPG-Starved Restaurants
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & grid x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: A load-sharing controller and optional battery lets Indian cloud kitchens and restaurants switch from scarce LPG to induction without waiting months for a utility load upgrade, then pools the fleet as a lunch-and-dinner-peak resource for DISCOMs.
customer: Cloud kitchens, small restaurant chains (5-50 outlets), hostel and office messes, caterers and sweet shops in Indian metros and tier-2 cities.
problem: The Hormuz-driven LPG shortage pushed induction cooktop demand up 20-25x and the government is distributing 500k stoves, but a commercial kitchen converting needs roughly 15-40 kW of extra connected load. DISCOM sanctioned-load upgrades and neighborhood transformers are slow and constrained, and the switch could add up to 27 GW of national demand at the evening peak. Low-income uptake is reported as sluggish because grid and financing are not ready.
solution: A CT-clamp controller (about $300-400) that sequences burners so total draw stays under the sanctioned load, since cooking tolerates duty-cycling. Add a 20-60 kWh LFP buffer to cover lunch and dinner peaks, financed as a monthly cooking-energy subscription through an NBFC and charged off-peak or on midday solar. The aggregated fleet later sells peak flexibility to DISCOMs under state demand-side management programs.
why_now: LPG scarcity is forcing commercial conversion now, stationary LFP packs are around $70/kWh, smart-meter and demand-side management programs are rolling out, and utilities cannot build capacity fast enough (transformer lead times, capex-biased regulation).
revenue_model: Controller sale of INR 25-35k, battery lease or subscription of roughly INR 15-30k per month (benchmarked against the commercial LPG bill it replaces, when LPG is available at all), and later DISCOM peak-flex payments per kW-year plus midday-charging arbitrage.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to electrifying cooking is not the stove but the permission to draw power at the kitchen's meter. A battery and a scheduler turn an infrastructure-approval problem into a financing problem. Cooking is a rare thermal load that can be shaped without harming the product, so the cheap controller does most of the work and generates the data that later sells flexibility.
first_30_days: Sell 10 controllers to cloud kitchens in one metro through restaurant associations and cloud-kitchen operator WhatsApp groups. Log load data and outages, then lease batteries to the first 3 with an NBFC partner. Use the aggregated load data to open a sandbox conversation with one DISCOM.

title: Collective Anti-Piracy Desk for 3D-Print Miniature Creators
angle: Pairing 1: Legal services, compliance & new regulations (EU AI Act, privacy, PFAS, right to repair, etc.) x Weird, niche and overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith communities, subcultures)
one_liner: A creator-owned enforcement collective that fingerprints STL/3D-print models, hunts leaks across Telegram, Discord and marketplaces, and uses EU Digital Services Act notice, trusted-flagger and appeal rights to make takedowns stick.
customer: Independent sculptors and small studios selling printable miniatures, terrain and tabletop models via Patreon, Kickstarter, MyMiniFactory, Cults3D and their own stores (tens of thousands worldwide, top creators earning six figures). Also indie designers of other collectible models (keyboard cases, cosplay props) and the hosting platforms that want a clean enforcement feed.
problem: Files leak within days of release, spread through Discord and Telegram, get resold on Etsy/eBay/Temu-style marketplaces and printed into physical minis. A solo creator faces hundreds of infringements a month, and one-by-one DMCA notices cost hours, are ignored or are countered by repeat offenders. Brand-protection vendors price for brands, not solo sculptors. The EU Digital Services Act gave structured levers (Art. 16 notice-and-action, Art. 17 statements of reasons, Art. 21 out-of-court dispute bodies, Art. 22 trusted-flagger priority) and put very large marketplaces such as Temu and AliExpress under Commission supervision, but nobody has packaged these levers for small creators.
solution: (1) Geometry-based mesh fingerprinting, robust to re-meshing, scaling, splitting and hollowing, plus image similarity for renders and prints, with crawlers for leak channels, marketplaces and cloud-drive links. (2) A case engine that files DMCA and DSA notices in correct legal form, tracks counter-notices and statements of reasons, and escalates repeat infringers to the platform's regulator complaint channels. (3) An EU-established entity built to apply for DSA trusted-flagger status; Art. 22 explicitly favors bodies that represent collective interests and are independent of platforms. (4) A 'legit copy' program that offers print farms and Etsy resellers a licensed route, so leaks become royalty income.
why_now: The printable-model economy on Patreon and 3D-printer adoption are at scale. The DSA has been fully applicable since Feb 2024 and the Commission's 2025 actions against Temu/AliExpress make regulator escalation credible (verify status). AI re-meshing and generative 3D tools make exact-hash detection obsolete. Pressure from IP owners like Games Workshop pushes hobbyists toward original designs, so creator-owned IP is growing.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $29-149/month by catalog size. 10-20% share of licensed royalties recovered from converted resellers. Enterprise feed for hosting platforms that want a vetted trusted-flagger channel.
non_obvious_insight: Piracy at this scale is a coordination problem. Thirty thousand creators each losing $5-50k cannot afford lawyers, but as a collective with formal DSA status they generate volume and quality that platforms must prioritise. The realistic prize is converting pirates into licensees (print farms reselling legally), not just takedown counts.
first_30_days: Sign 10 mid-tier Patreon sculptors for a free 30-day leak report. Build the fingerprint and crawler MVP with open-source mesh-hashing plus CLIP embeddings. Send DMCA/DSA notices through a part-time attorney and measure takedown rates. Convert reports to $49/month subscriptions. Register the EU entity and start the trusted-flagger application with counsel.

title: Pet Continuity Guarantee Funded by Shelters and Hospitals
one_liner: A membership that guarantees an older adult's pet is picked up within hours of a hospitalization and rehomed after death, paid for by the shelters and hospitals that currently absorb the cost.
customer: The payers are county animal-services agencies and shelters, hospital systems and Medicare Advantage plans, and Area Agencies on Aging. Seniors and their adult children pay a small membership.
problem: Seniors delay 911 calls, refuse admission and cut rehab short because 'nobody will feed Biscuit.' Social workers know it and nobody is paid to fix it. When the owner dies or is hospitalized long-term, the animal ends up as an owner surrender at an already crowded shelter. Nonprofit pet-guardianship programs (for example Friends of Strays) and some Meals on Wheels chapters offer emergency foster, but each is a local patchwork with no dispatch, no standard, and no way for a hospital to call at 2 a.m.
solution: Enrollment with a pet profile (vet records, medications, key-holder, behavior notes), a wallet card and a door sticker. A 24/7 dispatch line that ED nurses, discharge planners and EMS can call. A network of background-checked sitters and foster families paid per diem. A contract with a partner shelter for permanent placement, backed by a small pooled fund that acts as a pet trust in a box (roughly $1,500 per animal endowed from memberships and partner contributions). The system tracks response time and avoided surrenders, so a payer can see the return.
why_now: Shelters are running at or over capacity and paying more for intake. Hospitals are under pressure to cut ED boarding, length of stay and against-medical-advice discharges. A pet guardianship program was in the news in September 2025 (Forbes), signaling that shelters now see guardianship as core. About 4 million Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, and over half of adults 50+ own a pet (AARP).
revenue_model: B2G contract of $300-$800 per avoided surrender or per emergency placement. Hospital and health-plan fee of about $3-$6 per enrolled pet-owning member per month. Senior or family membership of $15-$25/month. Dispatch and sitter-coordination fees.
non_obvious_insight: She will never buy 'pet insurance.' She thinks of it as 'who takes Biscuit.' The barrier to care is emotional and logistical, and hospitals and shelters both pay for the consequences without seeing the link. Existing guardianship programs are capped not by adopters but by the lack of a 4-hour dispatch and response system.
first_30_days: Sign one county shelter and one hospital ED or social-work team as pilot partners. Enroll 50 seniors through Meals on Wheels routes and senior centers. Recruit 15 sitters from local sitter platforms with background checks. Track hours to placement and avoided surrenders, and use the numbers to close the first paid contract.

title: Delivery Robots for Gated Communities
one_liner: Buy the sidewalk-robot fleets that failed on public streets at a discount and run them inside senior-living, campus and large apartment communities as a subscription amenity.
customer: Operators of senior-living and continuing-care communities, hospital campuses, student housing, military bases and large HOAs. They pay a monthly amenity fee.
problem: Sidewalk delivery fails on demand density, not on technology. Serve built about 2,000 robots but booked $2.65M of 2025 revenue, roughly $1.3k per robot by my arithmetic. Meanwhile private communities are labor-squeezed and struggle to get meals, pharmacy items and packages to residents.
solution: Closed-loop robots on private paths deliver dining-hall meals, pharmacy pickups, mail and supplies within one campus. Use secondhand hardware, a light fleet-management layer, and teleop backup for edge cases. Price as a fixed monthly amenity fee plus a small per-delivery charge.
why_now: Sidewalk-delivery unit economics visibly broke in 2025-26, so hardware is cheap and experienced operators are available. Vision-language navigation cuts per-site mapping cost, and last-mile contractors are closing (4XH and Ardor), which shows how expensive human delivery labor has become.
revenue_model: $3-8k a month per community platform fee, plus $1-2 per delivery. Hardware is bundled or financed. Target 8-12 robots per community at about 60% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: A subscription amenity decouples revenue from order volume, which is exactly what killed the public-street model. A private campus also removes the permit, ADA and pedestrian-liability problems and guarantees density.
first_30_days: Pick 3 continuing-care or student-housing campuses in one metro. Buy or lease 3-5 used robots from a fleet operator raising cash. Run a teleop-assisted pilot delivering meals to about 20 residents, and convert one campus to a signed LOI at about $4k a month.

title: Notary Network as the Proof-of-Human Layer for Hiring
one_liner: Use the millions of already-commissioned notaries as in-person witnesses who certify that a remote job candidate is a real, physically present person and not a deepfake or proxy.
customer: Security and talent-acquisition leads at remote-first companies (50-2,000 employees) hiring engineers, finance and IT-admin roles, plus crypto and fintech firms, staffing agencies and BPOs onboarding remote workers. Paid per candidate.
problem: Real-time face-swap tools, proxy interviewees and North Korean IT-worker schemes (with DOJ takedowns of US 'laptop farms' in 2025) defeat video interviews and selfie-liveness KYC. Gartner has predicted that one in four candidate profiles could be fake by 2028. Big companies have reportedly brought back in-person final rounds, but a 60-person remote startup has no office to bring anyone to.
solution: A dispatch flow on top of existing mobile-notary and signing-agent networks. The candidate meets a notary in person, at a UPS Store, coworking space or their home. The notary checks physical ID and signs a jurat-style attestation, and the candidate's device is paired to a session key. The notary sits with them for the proctored final technical interview, or witnesses laptop receipt and first login. The employer receives a signed, legally meaningful 'Verified Human Presence' certificate to attach to the ATS, HRIS and payroll. Priced at $79-149 per candidate, with the notary paid $40-70.
why_now: Deepfake fraud in hiring became a mainstream security topic in 2025-26. Enforcement actions against laptop farms have made boards care. Remote-notary and mobile-notary dispatch marketplaces already have the workflow tooling, and ATS platforms now expose APIs and partner directories. Digital-identity vendors are all software-only and share the same weakness against generative video.
revenue_model: Per-verification fee; an ATS-integration subscription (Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever); annual re-verification for employees with privileged access; enterprise bundles for staffing agencies and BPOs.
non_obvious_insight: Notaries are the only large, already-bonded, already-commissioned network of humans whose legal job is to certify that a person was physically in front of them. Identity vendors overlooked them because they assumed software would replace presence. When faces become forgeable, presence attestation becomes the premium product, and the distribution network already exists and needs no capital to build.
first_30_days: Build a simple booking and attestation web flow. Sign up two mobile-notary networks or about 40 individual notaries across SF, NYC, Austin, Seattle and Chicago. Recruit 15-20 security-conscious remote-first startups through CISO and hiring-fraud communities. Charge $99 and complete 50 verifications. Publish anonymized 'fraud caught' case studies to drive inbound.

title: O-1 Evidence Vault as a Startup Employee Benefit
one_liner: Continuously captures, verifies and time-stamps the evidence that O-1A, EB-1A and NIW petitions are actually won on, so a lawyer can file in weeks instead of scrambling for six months.
customer: Venture-backed startups and AI labs with foreign-born staff pay $25-40 per employee per month. Founders, PhD students and researchers can use a self-serve tier. Immigration firms license a white-label version.
problem: The $100k fee on new H-1B petitions for workers abroad, and a wage-weighted lottery for everyone else, have pushed tech employers toward O-1A, EB-1A and NIW as the primary route. But these are evidence-driven cases. Clients show up with nothing organized, the lawyer spends weeks chasing citation counts, salary comparisons, press links and reference letters, letters end up as boilerplate, and half the evidence (paid associations, vanity press, generic membership) gets discounted by adjudicators at the final-merits stage anyway. AI-generated petitions are now a recognizable genre officers discount.
solution: A vault that connects to sources people already have (OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, GitHub/Hugging Face adoption, patents, OpenReview and conference reviewer rosters, Wayback-archived press, compensation data with consent) and adds structured quarterly manager memos documenting the employee's critical role. It logs each independent-expert letter request with dates and independence facts. Output is a criterion-by-criterion evidence map with gaps and a plain-language six-month plan, plus a flag for evidence types officers typically discount. It hands the packet to any immigration lawyer, including the employer's existing counsel.
why_now: The H-1B fee and lottery weighting since late 2025 have made O-1A and EB-1A a mainstream path rather than an exception for founders and stars. AI labs and startups need it for dozens of employees at once, so time-to-file matters. Public scholarly and code metadata are now available through open APIs, and LLMs make it feasible to structure messy evidence at low cost.
revenue_model: Per-employee SaaS ($25-40 per month), a $300-500 one-time evidence audit, and a licensing fee from law firms. Immigration counsel remains separate, and no fee-splitting occurs.
non_obvious_insight: Petitions are decided on what was already documented by the time the client met the lawyer. Nobody builds evidence continuously because no one owns the job: HR doesn't know the criteria, lawyers only engage after the decision to file, and employees don't know what counts. Separately, the evidence that counts (independent judging, real citations, critical-role documentation) is often free to collect early and impossible to fabricate later, while the paid pay-to-play tactics sold to nervous applicants are actively harmful.
first_30_days: Find 3 seed or Series A AI startups with heavily foreign-born teams, through their immigration counsel or investor platform teams. Run a manual concierge audit for 20 employees at $300 each, producing the criterion-by-criterion map in a spreadsheet plus Google Doc. Identify the top 5 recurring evidence gaps (they will be the same across companies) and automate those first. Convert the startups to a subscription once the first two employees file petitions faster than expected.

title: Pre-Procedure GLP-1 Readiness for Endoscopy and Ortho
one_liner: A 7-day workflow plus day-of gastric ultrasound that stops GLP-1 patients from being cancelled or aspirating at surgery centers.
customer: GI endoscopy centers, orthopedic groups, ASCs and their anesthesia groups.
problem: ASA reversed course in Oct 2024 and now advises most patients to continue GLP-1s, shifting the risk to residual gastric contents on the day. Centers cancel or abort cases, and 38% of GLP-1 users vs 8% of non-users were malnourished before joint surgery, which raises complication risk. There is no standard workflow, so every center improvises.
solution: Automated intake (drug, dose, indication, GI symptoms), tailored liquid-diet and hold instructions aligned to multi-society guidance, a malnutrition screen with a protein prehab plan, and nurse-performed gastric POCUS with AI-assisted antral grading and documentation on the day. Priced per case.
why_now: With ~22% of households containing a user, this is routine, not exceptional. Gastric POCUS studies are appearing (2025-26) and centers are looking for a defensible protocol after the 2024 guideline change.
revenue_model: $60-150 per GLP-1 patient case, plus anesthesia-group license and ultrasound rental.
non_obvious_insight: Centers will not stop scheduling GLP-1 patients, so the value is avoided same-day cancellations (thousands of dollars each) and defensible documentation. The buyer is the center's operations and anesthesia leadership, not the drug companies.
first_30_days: Sell to one endoscopy center and one anesthesia group. Supply paper-plus-SMS intake, protocols, a rented handheld ultrasound and training. Track cancellation rate before and after and price at $75 per case.

title: Orphan Bin Network: Leased Farm Storage Capacity
one_liner: Lease the thousands of idle grain bins left on consolidated and inherited farmsteads, retrofit them with cheap sensors, and run them as licensed satellite storage for co-ops.
customer: Co-ops and independent elevators that run short of upright storage every big harvest. Also landlord and heir bin owners who receive lease income. The elevator pays a per-bin SaaS fee plus a share of storage revenue.
problem: Upright storage is the co-op's hardest constraint, and building new capacity costs a huge multiple of leasing existing steel. Ground piles cost shrink and quality. Meanwhile farm consolidation and aging landowners leave many bins idle on rented farmsteads. Heirs pay taxes on stranded assets and have no way to monetize them. Iowa law already contemplates leased storage facilities under a warehouse license (the licensee simply notifies the state), but no one has packaged the monitoring, inventory verification and paperwork to make it routine.
solution: A 'bin-in-a-box' program run under the co-op's existing warehouse license. Sign multi-year leases with owners and install a retrofit kit: temperature and moisture cables, fill-level sensors, aeration control and a remote camera. Wire it into the co-op's grain accounting system so receipts, inventory and shrink tracking work like any owned bin. Provide the compliance package (state notifications, insurance riders, inspection logs, an auditor-ready trail). This is not a marketplace. The co-op stays the licensed warehouseman and the bin owner becomes a landlord.
why_now: The 2025 record harvest left the top 12 corn states about 1.4 billion bushels short of upright storage, according to CoBank analysis, and low prices keep grain in storage longer. Elevators piled grain on the ground and rented temporary space. Cheap LoRa and cellular bin sensors now cost far less than a few years ago, and 2026 harvest is starting.
revenue_model: SaaS of about $250 to $500 per bin per year plus install margin on the sensor kit. 10% to 20% share of incremental storage revenue. Optional financing spread on kit costs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not steel but licensed, monitored, insurable steel. Idle bins already exist by the thousands. What is missing is the trust layer (sensors, chain-of-custody and a bonded warehouseman) that lets an elevator sign for grain sitting in someone else's yard.
first_30_days: Pick one co-op that just piled grain on the ground. Identify 10 idle bins within 15 miles from the co-op's landlord and ag-lending contacts. Confirm the notification steps with the Iowa Grain Warehouse Bureau. Install sensor kits on 5 bins before harvest peak and store real grain for the first time this season.

title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.

title: Independent Service Roll-Up for Lab Robots
one_liner: Roll up independent service shops for liquid handlers and lab robots, using remote diagnostics and pooled parts to undercut OEM contracts for squeezed academic cores and CROs.
customer: Academic core facilities, small biotechs and CROs running Hamilton, Tecan, Beckman, Agilent and Opentrons fleets; later autonomous-lab operators who need uptime.
problem: NIH turbulence (a grant-cap proposal, stripped grants-staff protections, K99 visa limits) squeezes core budgets. OEM service contracts typically run about 8-12% of list price per year (an estimate) and OEMs prioritize pharma customers. Layoffs at biotechs and tool vendors free skilled field engineers. Downtime costs more as labs become automated.
solution: Flat-fee per-robot subscriptions at 30-40% below OEM, remote log ingestion with AI triage of error codes, a shared refurbished-parts pool sourced from wind-downs, and uptime guarantees. Acquire 2-4 small independent service shops at 3-5x EBITDA to get technicians and customers.
why_now: STAT tracks ongoing NIH instability. Biopharma layoffs (15,000+) and shuttered labs supply both engineers and used parts. More robots are being installed for AI-directed workflows.
revenue_model: $8-30k per robot per year at 55-65% gross margin on contracts, plus parts and time-and-materials, plus multiple arbitrage on acquired shops.
non_obvious_insight: Automation's bottleneck is uptime, not capability. Agent-run labs make downtime costlier, and robot telemetry lets an independent shop beat the OEM on mean time to repair. Wind-down biotechs are a parts supply the OEMs do not control.
first_30_days: Hire 2 ex-OEM field engineers. Sign 5-8 academic cores in one metro at introductory pricing. Buy used spares from wind-downs. Build a log-parsing dashboard for Hamilton and Tecan error logs.

title: Pay-Per-Attendance Social Prescriptions for Loneliness
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare delivery/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Mental health/loneliness/community/meaning
one_liner: A settlement layer where health systems and employers pay small local groups (Men's Sheds, choirs, walking clubs) a fixed fee for every verified attendance by a doctor-referred lonely patient.
customer: Nonprofit-hospital community-benefit and population-health teams and self-insured employers first, then Medicare Advantage plans. The suppliers who get paid are local groups: Men's Sheds, choirs, run and walking clubs, craft circles.
problem: Social prescribing works abroad (Merton, London: GP visits down 33%, A&E visits down 50%) and WHO now attributes about 871k deaths a year to isolation. The US has no reimbursement path, so PCPs with 31-day waits have nowhere to send lonely patients. Third places run on volunteers and charity, and referral directories list them without paying them. Loneliness programs fail on retention, because people stop showing up after week 2.
solution: Screen for loneliness in primary care or at employer open enrollment (UCLA-3 or a similar short scale). The clinician sends an e-referral to a vetted local group, and the patient checks in by QR or NFC at each session. The buyer pays the group $8-15 per verified attendance, capped per member per month, and the platform keeps 15-20%. A dashboard tracks show rate at weeks 4 and 8, loneliness score change and ED or visit utilization. It is a payment and verification rail, not a social network. Groups are paid to be welcoming and to keep people coming, which is the opposite of an engagement-maximizing app.
why_now: WHO's June 2025 Commission report made loneliness a measured global health metric. Dating and social apps are stalling (Bumble layoffs, BFF relaunch), so friendship demand has no monetized supply. Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027 and lapsed ACA subsidies are squeezing hospital margins and pushing systems toward cheap prevention with measurable ROI. Employers are also cutting expensive drug benefits and looking for low-cost wellbeing spend.
revenue_model: Per-verified-attendance settlement (buyer pays, group gets about 80-85%), plus a small PMPM or annual platform fee for the outcome dashboard and clinic workflow. Later, Medicare Advantage supplemental-benefit contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not loneliness interventions. It is a business model for the hosts. A health payer already pays 10-100x $10 per avoided ED visit, and paying per attendance turns retention (the real failure point) into the unit of revenue. Referral directories like Findhelp route people but do not pay, and hosts cannot survive on referrals alone.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 small groups in one metro and sign each to a $10-per-attendance pilot. Sign one health-system community-benefit office or one self-insured employer for 100 referrals. Build check-in with a QR code and a spreadsheet-backed dashboard, no app needed. Measure week-4 show rate against the roughly 20-30% typical of unpaid programs, then use that number to pitch the second buyer.

title: Incretin-in-a-Drop Assay for Life Underwriting
one_liner: A dried-blood-spot or oral-fluid lab test that tells insurers whether an applicant is actually on semaglutide, tirzepatide, orforglipron or retatrutide.
customer: Life and disability insurers, reinsurers, MGAs and paramedical exam vendors, with bariatric programs, trial sponsors and outcome-based employer programs as follow-on buyers.
problem: Cash-pay and direct-ship fills (LillyDirect, NovoCare, telehealth-partner pharmacies, compounders, gray market) are only partly visible in claims-based Rx histories, so BMI looks 'preferred' while drug-supported. Stopping the drug means rebound and adverse selection. Gray-market retatrutide is invisible by design.
solution: A validated LC-MS/MS panel (semaglutide, tirzepatide, orforglipron, cagrilintide, retatrutide) run by a partner CLIA lab as an add-on to the paramedical exam, returning 'on-board, recent use or none'. Later expansions to pre-op verification, adherence-verified outcome contracts and a consumer 'proof of adherence' report.
why_now: Published LC-MS/MS methods for semaglutide and tirzepatide matured in 2026, the FDA's LDT rule was vacated in 2025, and cash-pay pill volume exploded in 2026 (Wegovy pill >2M scripts).
revenue_model: $25-45 per test as an underwriting add-on, volume tiers for carriers, and later $79 consumer or clinician tests.
non_obvious_insight: This is the first mass-market chronic drug that bypasses the industry's data plumbing. Underwriters will pay for direct measurement over questionnaires because the cost of a wrong mortality class is far above $35.
first_30_days: Ask two Rx-history vendors what share of DTC fills they see. Contract a CLIA tox lab to validate an assay from published methods. Pitch 10 MGAs and reinsurer innovation teams, and run a paid 200-sample blinded pilot with one friendly insurer, with consent and state unfair-discrimination rules reviewed by counsel.
